teaching.causalExplanation: It's zero. The standard enthalpy of formation, delta H f, is the enthalpy change when one mole of a compound forms from its elements, with every substance in its standard state. That's its most stable form at one hundred kilopascals and a stated temperature, here twenty-five degrees, like oxygen gas, carbon as graphite, and liquid water. Making oxygen gas from oxygen gas changes nothing, so every element in its standard state has a formation enthalpy of zero. A formation equation always makes exactly one mole of the compound, even if that means fractions in front of the elements. For ammonia, it's half a nitrogen plus one and a half hydrogen, minus forty-six point one. For liquid ethanol, it's two carbon, three hydrogen and half an oxygen, minus two hundred and seventy-seven point seven. The state matters too. Liquid water is minus two hundred and eighty-five point eight, but steam is only minus two hundred and forty-one point eight. Think of the elements as sea level. Each compound's formation enthalpy is its height above or below that level. Most compounds sit below, because forming them releases energy, but a few, like ethene, sit above. Once every substance has a height measured from the same sea level, any reaction's delta H is just the difference in height.

scenes.teachingReason: Here's why that works. Imagine an indirect route. First, break the reactants back down into their elements. That's the reverse of forming them, so its delta H is minus the reactants' formation enthalpies. Then build the products from those same elements, which adds the products' formation enthalpies. By Hess's law, that route gives the same delta H as the reaction itself. So it's products minus reactants.
